lupus.name: Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)
lupus.definition: A long-term autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue, most often causing joint aches, skin rashes and tiredness.
lupus.overview: Lupus is a lasting autoimmune illness in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue. It is most often marked by joint aches, skin rashes and fatigue, and symptoms vary from person to person and can come and go. It is more common in women. There is no cure, but symptoms can improve if treatment starts early.
causes: Autoimmune: the immune system attacks healthy tissue
The exact trigger is unclear
Possible contributors named by the NHS include viral infections, certain medicines, sunlight, puberty, childbirth and the menopause

lupus.diagnosis: No single test confirms lupus, so doctors combine the person's history, a physical examination and laboratory tests. A GP usually starts with blood tests, and lupus may be diagnosed if they show a high level of a certain type of antibody together with typical symptoms. Urine and blood tests, and sometimes a kidney biopsy, may be used when the kidneys might be affected. Scans of the heart, kidneys or other organs may follow if they seem affected.

The NHS lists anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, hydroxychloroquine for fatigue, skin and joint problems, and steroids for kidney inflammation and rashes. sections.heading: What are the symptoms of lupus?
sections.body:
Lupus symptoms vary from person to person. The NHS lists joint and muscle pain and extreme tiredness that does not go away however much a person rests as main symptoms. A rash often appears across the nose and cheeks and can be triggered by sunlight. NIAMS describes this as a butterfly-shaped rash.

Other possible signs include headaches, mouth ulcers, fever, hair loss, weight loss and swollen glands. Some people have Raynaud's, where the fingers and toes change colour. Arthritis in lupus can cause painful, swollen joints and morning stiffness. The NHS says lupus often flares up, with symptoms becoming worse for a few weeks or sometimes longer. Lupus can also affect organs such as the kidneys, heart, lungs and brain.

sections.heading: What causes lupus and who gets it?
sections.body:
Lupus is an autoimmune condition, which means the immune system attacks healthy tissue. Lupus UK explains that the immune system becomes overactive and makes antibodies against the body's own cells, and inflammation can then affect the skin, joints and other tissues. The NHS says lupus is not contagious.

The causes are not fully understood, but the NHS lists possible triggers including viral infections, certain medicines, sunlight, puberty, childbirth and the menopause. The NHS says lupus is more common in women and in people of African, Caribbean, Asian or Chinese background. Lupus UK describes the course as variable, with flares and remission, and says the disease lasts many years in most people.

sections.heading: How is lupus diagnosed?
sections.body:
Because the symptoms overlap with other conditions, diagnosis can take time. No single test confirms lupus, and doctors combine the person's history, a physical examination and laboratory tests.

A GP usually starts with blood tests. NIAMS says a positive ANA (antinuclear antibody) test is common in lupus but does not confirm it, because healthy people can also have a positive result. The NHS says lupus may be diagnosed if tests show a high level of a certain type of antibody and the person also has the typical symptoms. NIDDK says lupus nephritis, which is kidney involvement, is diagnosed through urine and blood tests and sometimes a kidney biopsy. Scans of the heart, kidneys or other organs may follow if they seem to be affected.

sections.heading: How is lupus treated?
sections.body:
There is no cure for lupus, but the NHS says symptoms can improve if treatment starts early. Lupus UK says treatment aims to keep the disease controlled to reduce the chance of a flare.

Options named by the NHS include anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, hydroxychloroquine for fatigue, skin and joint problems, and steroids for kidney inflammation and rashes. For severe cases, immunosuppressant or biological medicines may be used. NIAMS mentions a biologic medicine that blocks the type I interferon receptor and may improve skin, joint and overall lupus symptoms. NIAMS advises working with a doctor to decide the best treatment plan and taking medicines as prescribed. The NHS self-care advice for people with lupus includes sun protection, pacing yourself, staying active and managing stress.

sections.heading: Living with lupus: flares and self-care
sections.body:
Lupus UK describes the course as variable. Some people have one flare, while others have periods of increased disease activity followed by remission, and many flares are mild. NIAMS lists increased tiredness, joint swelling, pain, rash, fever, abdominal pain and headache as common warning signs of a flare. It says spotting these warning signs can help a person prevent a flare or make the symptoms less severe, and that sun exposure and stress can trigger flares.

The NHS self-care advice includes sun protection, pacing yourself, staying active and managing stress. Sun protection includes a high-factor sunscreen and a hat. NHS 111 Wales also advises against smoking, which it says makes lupus worse. NIAMS says many people with lupus lead happy lives.

sections.heading: What complications can lupus cause?
sections.body:
Severity varies, and a severe case can cause serious inflammation of the heart, lungs, brain or kidneys. Lupus nephritis is inflammation of the kidneys, and Great Ormond Street Hospital says it can in a few cases progress to kidney failure. Lupus UK says kidney disease in lupus needs careful monitoring because it can cause no symptoms, and NIDDK says it is found through urine and blood tests and sometimes a biopsy.

Lupus UK says many women with lupus have successful pregnancies, and that stable disease before conception makes a stable pregnancy more likely. It also says lupus pregnancies can sometimes end in miscarriage or stillbirth, that some women have flares during pregnancy and need careful observation, and that lupus may sometimes affect fertility. Lupus UK also discusses pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy complication, and advises that individual pregnancy questions are discussed with a specialist.

faqs.q: Is lupus contagious?
faqs.a: No, lupus is not contagious. It is an autoimmune condition, in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue. The exact trigger is unclear, but the NHS lists possible contributors including viral infections, certain medicines, sunlight, puberty, childbirth and the menopause. These are possible contributors to developing lupus, not ways of catching it from another person.

faqs.q: Can lupus be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure for lupus, according to the NHS. The NHS says symptoms can improve if treatment starts early. Lupus UK says treatment aims to keep the disease controlled to reduce the chance of a flare. The NHS lists anti-inflammatory painkillers, hydroxychloroquine and steroids, with immunosuppressant or biological medicines for severe cases.

faqs.q: What is the outlook for people with lupus?
faqs.a: Lupus UK says the outlook for survival has improved in recent years, and that with early treatment lupus may settle and ultimately go into remission. The course is variable: some people have one flare, while others have periodic increased disease activity followed by remission. A rheumatologist or lupus specialist can discuss what this means for an individual.

faqs.q: Can women with lupus have a baby?
faqs.a: Lupus UK says many women with lupus have successful pregnancies, and that stable disease before conception makes a stable pregnancy more likely. It also says lupus pregnancies can sometimes end in miscarriage or stillbirth, and that some women have flares during pregnancy and need careful observation. Questions about pregnancy are best discussed with a rheumatologist or lupus specialist.

faqs.q: When should I see a doctor about possible lupus?
faqs.a: The NHS advises seeing a GP if lupus symptoms occur often, and says symptoms can improve if treatment starts early. Joint and muscle pain, extreme tiredness that rest does not ease, and a rash across the nose and cheeks are among the main symptoms. A routine GP appointment is the usual first step. Severe or sudden symptoms, such as chest pain, need urgent help through NHS 111 or the GP the same day, or 999 in an emergency.

fibromyalgia.name: Fibromyalgia
fibromyalgia.definition: A long-term condition that causes pain all over the body.
fibromyalgia.overview: Fibromyalgia, also called fibromyalgia syndrome, is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body. The NHS says increased sensitivity to pain, muscle stiffness, poor sleep, fatigue and difficulty concentrating are common. It is more common in women than in men and usually starts in midlife, according to the NHS. The exact cause is unknown and there is no specific test, but treatments can help relieve some of the symptoms.
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Abnormal levels of certain chemicals in the brain are thought to be involved
Changes in the way the central nervous system processes pain messages
Genetic factors, as the condition tends to run in families
Triggers such as injury, infection or stress may play a part
riskFactors: A common link with arthritis and with a traumatic event, according to Versus Arthritis
signs: Blood, urine and imaging tests are typically normal
Widespread pain with other symptoms such as fatigue and poor sleep
complications: Low mood or depression can accompany the condition
Other pain conditions can exist alongside it
fibromyalgia.diagnosis: There is no specific test for fibromyalgia, the NHS says. NIAMS says it is diagnosed mainly from widespread pain together with other symptoms. MedlinePlus says the provider reviews the history, examines the person and may order tests to exclude other conditions with similar symptoms.
fibromyalgia.treatment: There is no cure, and the NHS says the main treatments are exercise, talking therapies and medicines. Antidepressants are sometimes used to relieve pain. NIAMS describes a plan combining psychological and behavioural therapy, medicines and self-management such as physical exercise, yoga or tai chi. Anti-inflammatory pain relievers are usually not effective for fibromyalgia, according to NIAMS.
fibromyalgia.prevention: The sources reviewed do not describe a way to prevent fibromyalgia; self-management steps such as staying active, good sleep habits and managing stress are described for living with it.
fibromyalgia.seekCare: The NHS advises seeing a GP, through a routine appointment, if a person thinks they have fibromyalgia. NHS-based guidance suggests getting in touch again if pain is getting worse, self-help has not helped after several weeks, or new symptoms appear. Call 999 for an emergency, and use NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment for urgent problems.

sections.heading: What is fibromyalgia?
sections.body:
Fibromyalgia, also called fibromyalgia syndrome, is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body. Versus Arthritis describes it as not a problem of the joints, bones or muscles themselves. It says that, unlike in conditions such as arthritis, the pain is not caused by visible inflammation or damage to the body, and that this does not mean the symptoms are unreal. The charity adds that the exact cause is unclear.

The NHS says it is more common in women than in men and usually starts in midlife, although it can affect people of any age, including children and older people. Versus Arthritis says most cases begin between the mid-20s and mid-50s. The US National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS) says that anyone can get fibromyalgia, although more women than men are affected. Symptoms can change over time. There is currently no cure, but treatment can ease some symptoms, although the NHS says they are unlikely to disappear completely.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of fibromyalgia?
sections.body:
The NHS lists increased sensitivity to pain, muscle stiffness, poor sleep and fatigue among the common symptoms. It also describes problems with concentration and memory, known as fibro-fog, as well as headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, and feelings of frustration, worry or low mood. MedlinePlus describes a similar picture of widespread pain, sleep problems, fatigue and trouble with thinking and memory.

MedlinePlus also lists numbness or tingling and sensitivity to light, noise, odours and temperature among the main symptoms. The NHS says symptoms can get better or worse depending on factors such as stress levels, changes in the weather or how physically active a person is. Because the symptoms can be similar to those of a number of other conditions, the NHS says there is no specific test to confirm the diagnosis, and a GP diagnoses it by looking at the symptoms and their effect on daily life.

sections.heading: What causes fibromyalgia, and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
The NHS says the exact cause is unknown. It says the condition is thought to be related to abnormal levels of certain chemicals in the brain and to changes in the way the central nervous system processes pain messages. The NHS adds that genes may play a part, and that the condition often appears to be triggered by physical or emotional events such as an injury, an infection or stress.

NIAMS says the condition tends to run in families, so genetic factors are likely to contribute, although little is known for certain about the specific genes involved. It also says researchers think environmental factors play a role. Mood disorders may make fibromyalgia more likely, according to NIAMS. Versus Arthritis notes a common link with arthritis, a traumatic event, and mental health and wellbeing, and says fibromyalgia is not caused by damage or an injury to the body.

sections.heading: How is fibromyalgia diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no specific test for fibromyalgia, and that a GP diagnoses it by looking at the symptoms and their effect on daily life. NIAMS says the diagnosis is made mainly from widespread pain together with other symptoms. MedlinePlus says providers have to rule out other causes of the symptoms: the provider reviews the history in detail, examines the person and may order X-rays and blood tests to exclude other conditions.

MedlinePlus adds that blood, urine and imaging tests are typically normal in fibromyalgia and are ordered to check for conditions with similar symptoms. The CDC says a health care provider may suggest working with a team of specialists, which can include a rheumatologist, pain management specialist, physical therapist, mental health professional and sleep specialist. NIAMS says primary care providers manage most people with fibromyalgia, with pain management specialists also part of the team. NICE describes fibromyalgia (chronic widespread pain) as a type of chronic primary pain, meaning pain with no clear underlying cause, or pain, or its impact, out of proportion to any observable injury or disease.

sections.heading: How is fibromyalgia treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main treatments are exercise, talking therapies and medicines. It says antidepressants are sometimes used to relieve pain, and that cognitive behavioural therapy is a common talking therapy. NIAMS describes a plan that typically combines psychological and behavioural therapy, medicines and self-management approaches such as physical exercise and movement therapies like yoga or tai chi. The CDC lists cognitive behavioural therapy, a type of talk therapy meant to change how people act or think.

NIAMS says a number of medicines can help relieve pain and improve sleep, and that improvement is often gradual. It adds that anti-inflammatory pain relievers are usually not effective, because fibromyalgia does not cause tissue inflammation, although they may help with other painful conditions. Versus Arthritis says a doctor may only recommend drug treatment once options such as exercise, psychological therapy or acupuncture have been tried. For chronic primary pain, NICE guideline NG193 recommends offering a supervised group exercise programme to people aged 16 and over, and considering an antidepressant for adults after a full discussion of the benefits and risks.

sections.heading: What can help with living with fibromyalgia day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS self-help page says relaxation is important and suggests that deep breathing or meditation may help. It also notes that stress can make symptoms flare and that relaxing before bed may help sleep, and it lists sleep habits such as getting up at the same time each morning, keeping a bedtime routine, and avoiding caffeine, nicotine and alcohol before bed. Versus Arthritis links poor sleep with the condition and says regular activity, particularly aerobic exercise, and cognitive behavioural therapy have been effective for people with disrupted sleep.

A University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust page cautions that letting symptoms alone guide activity levels can lead to a boom-and-bust cycle of being over-active and under-active. A Torbay and South Devon NHS leaflet says it is important to pace yourself in any activity. The CDC lists learning self-management skills, regular physical activity and keeping a healthy weight as recommended strategies. For fibro-fog, an NHS hospital pain-clinic workbook suggests keeping notes in one place, such as a notepad or phone, and breaking tasks into smaller chunks.

sections.heading: When should someone see a doctor about fibromyalgia?
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if a person thinks they have fibromyalgia, and a routine GP appointment is the usual route.

NHS-based guidance suggests getting back in touch if pain is getting worse, if self-help measures have not helped after several weeks, if prescribed medicine is not helping, or if new symptoms appear. The same guidance advises that anyone who thinks they may be depressed should get help from a GP. If someone feels in immediate danger from thoughts of harming themselves, calling 999 is the route, and NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time, can also be used. For sudden severe symptoms that do not fit the usual pattern, such as chest pain or weakness on one side, call 999; NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment is the route for urgent problems that are not emergencies.

faqs.q: Can fibromyalgia be cured?
faqs.a: There is currently no cure for fibromyalgia, the NHS says. Treatments can help relieve some of the symptoms, although they are unlikely to disappear completely. The main treatments the NHS describes are exercise, talking therapies and medicines, and symptoms can get better or worse over time depending on factors such as stress, weather and activity.

faqs.q: Is fibromyalgia the same as arthritis?
faqs.a: No. Versus Arthritis says fibromyalgia is not a problem of the joints, bones or muscles themselves. It says the pain is not caused by visible inflammation or damage to the body, unlike in conditions such as arthritis. The charity also notes a common link between fibromyalgia and arthritis, among other factors.

faqs.q: Does fibromyalgia show up on blood tests or scans?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no specific test for fibromyalgia. MedlinePlus says blood, urine and imaging tests are typically normal in fibromyalgia and are ordered to check for conditions with similar symptoms. NIAMS says diagnosis rests mainly on widespread pain together with other symptoms.

faqs.q: Does exercise help fibromyalgia?
faqs.a: The NHS lists exercise among the main treatments for fibromyalgia. NIAMS includes physical exercise and movement therapies such as yoga or tai chi in the self-management part of a treatment plan, and NICE recommends offering supervised group exercise for chronic primary pain. A University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust page warns of a boom-and-bust cycle of being over-active and under-active.

vertigo.name: Vertigo and balance problems (including BPPV and Meniere's disease)
vertigo.definition: Vertigo is the feeling that you, or the world around you, is moving or spinning, and it is often caused by a problem in the inner ear.
vertigo.overview: The NHS describes vertigo as a symptom rather than a condition in itself. Inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes, and the NHS lists benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease among them. BPPV causes brief, intense spells of vertigo triggered by a change in head position, while Ménière's disease involves episodes of vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in the ear. Most people with vertigo improve without treatment, and treatment depends on the cause.
causes: Inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes of vertigo.
Common causes listed by the NHS are BPPV, labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease.
In BPPV, loose otoconia tumble into one of the semicircular canals and affect how the cupula works.
The cause of Ménière's disease is unknown according to MedlinePlus, and the NIDCD says theories about the cause vary.
signs: Involuntary eye movements called nystagmus, with vertigo, when the Dix-Hallpike head-position test is carried out in BPPV
complications: BPPV can recur, and in some people it becomes a persistent or recurrent problem
Hearing loss in Ménière's disease
vertigo.diagnosis: BPPV is diagnosed mainly from the history of symptoms and from typical findings on the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre, a head-position test. For Ménière's disease, no single test confirms the diagnosis, which rests on the pattern of recurring attacks and hearing tests. For suspected Ménière's disease, the NHS says a GP will check the ears, head and neck.
vertigo.treatment: Treatment depends on the cause; for vertigo in general the NHS says antihistamines can sometimes help and balance exercises may be recommended. BPPV often settles by itself or with canalith repositioning manoeuvres done in a clinic. Ménière's disease cannot be cured, but treatment can help the symptoms, and the NIDCD says diet changes, stopping smoking and anti-vertigo or anti-nausea medicines may be recommended. NHS 111 Wales says surgery on the inner ear is rarely offered, when symptoms are hard to control.
vertigo.prevention: The NHS suggests lifestyle changes such as drinking plenty of fluids, avoiding caffeine, not smoking and not drinking alcohol can help manage Ménière's disease.
vertigo.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for double or lost vision, hearing loss, difficulty speaking, or weakness, numbness or tingling in the limbs with vertigo. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised by the NHS when vertigo comes with a severe headache, sickness or a high temperature. A routine GP appointment is advised if vertigo will not go away or keeps coming back.

sections.heading: What is vertigo, and what causes it?
sections.body:
Vertigo is the feeling that you, or the environment around you, is moving or spinning. The NHS describes it as a symptom rather than a condition in itself. Attacks can be short, and sometimes they last much longer. Inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes. The NHS lists benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease as common causes.

The NHS describes BPPV as one of the most common causes of vertigo. Most people with vertigo improve without treatment, and what is done depends on the cause. This page looks mainly at BPPV and Ménière's disease, two inner ear conditions that the NHS and the US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) describe.

sections.heading: What is BPPV and how does it feel?
sections.body:
The NIDCD describes BPPV as a brief, intense episode of vertigo triggered by a specific change in the position of the head. The NHS likewise says specific head movements can bring on the vertigo. The NIDCD gives examples such as bending down, tilting the head to look up or over a shoulder, or rolling over in bed. It says BPPV can follow a head injury or develop simply with age.

An NIDCD handout explains that the condition arises when loose otoconia tumble into one of the semicircular canals and affect how the cupula works. Otoconia are tiny crystals in the inner ear, and the semicircular canals are the fluid-filled loops that sense head movement. A medical review says BPPV is frequently resolved on its own or through canalith repositioning manoeuvres carried out in a clinic. StatPearls, an online medical reference, describes the overall outlook as favourable. The review adds that the course can range from a problem that is treated simply to one that persists or recurs and causes disability. NICE guideline NG127 notes that BPPV is common after a head injury or labyrinthitis.

sections.heading: What is Ménière's disease?
sections.body:
The NIDCD describes Ménière's disease as episodes of vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus (a ringing or buzzing in the ear) and a feeling of fullness in the ear. The NHS lists feeling that you or everything around you is spinning, losing your balance and hearing loss among the symptoms.

An NHS Lanarkshire page says attacks usually last a few hours. It adds that the symptoms can be very troublesome and worrying. The NIDCD links Ménière's disease with a fluid imbalance in the labyrinth, a part of the inner ear, caused by a build-up of a fluid called endolymph. It says theories vary about what causes the condition, and MedlinePlus says the cause is unknown. The NHS says Ménière's disease cannot be cured, but treatment can help with the symptoms.

sections.heading: How is vertigo diagnosed?
sections.body:
For BPPV, diagnosis rests mainly on the history of symptoms and on typical findings during the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre, a head-position test. NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries (CKS) says posterior canal BPPV is diagnosed if the manoeuvre provokes vertigo and torsional, upbeating nystagmus, which means involuntary eye movements. NICE guideline NG127 recommends offering the Hallpike manoeuvre to adults with brief rotational vertigo triggered by head movement, if a trained health professional is available, and offering canalith repositioning if BPPV is diagnosed.

For Ménière's disease, no single test confirms the diagnosis. It rests on the pattern of recurring attacks and on hearing tests, and diagnostic criteria require more than one episode of vertigo. The NHS says a GP will check the ears, head and neck when Ménière's disease is suspected. NG127 also asks clinicians to be alert to vestibular migraine, which is migraine-associated vertigo, in adults with episodes of dizziness lasting from 5 minutes to 72 hours and a history of recurrent headache. For sudden-onset acute vestibular syndrome, NG127 advises immediate referral unless BPPV or postural hypotension explains the problem.

sections.heading: How are BPPV and Ménière's disease treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment for vertigo depends on the cause. It adds that antihistamines can sometimes help and that balance exercises may be recommended. For BPPV, NHS patient leaflets describe the Epley manoeuvre, a series of four head movements, as a treatment. NICE guideline NG127 recommends offering canalith repositioning when BPPV is diagnosed, if a trained health professional is available.

For Ménière's disease, the NHS says treatment mainly eases symptoms, with medicines for dizziness and nausea, and that tinnitus may also need treatment. The NIDCD says a specialist ear, nose and throat doctor (otolaryngologist) may recommend changes to diet and, for smokers, stopping smoking. It adds that anti-vertigo or anti-nausea medicines may relieve symptoms, though they can cause drowsiness. NHS 111 Wales says surgery on the inner ear is rarely offered, when symptoms are hard to control.

sections.heading: Self-care, living with vertigo and when to get help
sections.body:
For vertigo attacks, the NHS suggests lying still in a dark room, sitting down as soon as dizziness begins, and getting up slowly after lying down. It also suggests a walking stick for people at risk of falling. For Ménière's disease, the NHS says drinking lots of fluids, avoiding caffeine, not smoking and not drinking alcohol can help manage it.

A routine GP appointment is advised by the NHS if vertigo does not go away or keeps coming back. An urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 is advised if vertigo comes with a severe headache, sickness or a high temperature. Call 999 or go to A&E if vertigo comes with double or lost vision, hearing loss, difficulty speaking, or weakness, numbness or tingling in the limbs.

faqs.q: Is vertigo the same as dizziness?
faqs.a: Vertigo is the feeling that you or your surroundings are moving or spinning. The NHS describes it as a symptom rather than a condition in itself. Inner ear problems are the most common causes, and the NHS lists BPPV, labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis and Ménière's disease. Treatment depends on the cause, and most people improve without treatment.

faqs.q: Does BPPV go away on its own?
faqs.a: A medical review says BPPV is frequently resolved on its own or through canalith repositioning manoeuvres done in a clinic. StatPearls describes the overall outlook as favourable, and the review notes that the problem can persist or recur in some people. The NHS advises a routine GP appointment if vertigo will not go away or keeps coming back.

faqs.q: Can Ménière's disease be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says Ménière's disease cannot be cured, but treatment can help with the symptoms. MedlinePlus says the cause is unknown, and the NIDCD says theories about the cause vary. Treatment may include diet changes, stopping smoking and medicines for vertigo or nausea, according to the NIDCD. NHS 111 Wales says surgery is rarely offered.

faqs.q: What is the difference between BPPV and Ménière's disease?
faqs.a: The NIDCD describes BPPV as a brief, intense episode of vertigo triggered by a specific change in head position. It describes Ménière's disease as episodes of vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in the ear. The NHS also lists loss of balance and hearing loss among the symptoms of Ménière's disease.

faqs.q: When should vertigo be treated as an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if vertigo comes with double or lost vision, hearing loss, difficulty speaking, or limb weakness, numbness or tingling. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for vertigo with a severe headache, sickness or a high temperature.

sections.heading: What is lactose intolerance?
sections.body:
Lactose is the sugar found in milk and dairy foods. Lactose intolerance means digestive trouble, such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas, after eating or drinking foods that contain it. It is tied to lactase, the enzyme that breaks lactose down. MedlinePlus says it develops when the small intestine does not make enough of this enzyme.

It is a different condition from a milk allergy, which the NHS describes separately. Tolerance varies, and NIDDK says many people may not need to avoid every food that contains lactose. The NHS says most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet. The NHS also says a lactase supplement taken before food or drink that contains lactose may help some people, and NIDDK describes lactase tablets or drops that contain the enzyme that breaks down lactose.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of lactose intolerance?
sections.body:
The NHS lists common symptoms including stomach pain or discomfort, bloating, wind, rumbling in the stomach, diarrhoea or constipation, and nausea. The NHS says they can begin anywhere from minutes to hours after eating lactose, and MedlinePlus says they often occur 30 minutes to 2 hours after having milk products.

Other conditions can cause similar symptoms. MedlinePlus lists irritable bowel syndrome, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease and small bowel bacterial overgrowth as examples. The NHS advises seeing a GP if symptoms keep coming back, especially after eating, or if there is blood in the stool or unexplained weight loss. A routine GP appointment is the usual route. The NHS also advises seeing a GP before removing dairy from a child's diet, and warns against removing foods from anyone's diet without advice from a GP or dietitian.

sections.heading: What causes lactose intolerance?
sections.body:
The NHS says the most common cause is the body producing too little lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose. It can also follow bowel conditions, infections, surgery or injury. MedlinePlus says surgery on the small intestine, infections in the small intestine (most often in children) and diseases that damage the small intestine, such as coeliac disease or Crohn disease, can lead to it. A rarer cause is a genetic variant present from birth.

MedlinePlus Genetics describes lactase nonpersistence, the gradual fall in lactase activity after infancy, as occurring in most people. It says this is most prevalent in people of East Asian descent and also very common in people of West African, Arab, Jewish, Greek and Italian descent. Some premature babies are lactose intolerant, and the condition usually improves without treatment as the baby gets older.

MedlinePlus says that when a temporary diarrhoeal illness was the trigger, lactase levels return to normal within a few weeks. A UK NHS clinical guidance page describes intolerance after gastroenteritis as mainly temporary.

sections.heading: How is lactose intolerance diagnosed?
sections.body:
A doctor typically starts by asking about symptoms, medical history and eating habits. The NHS says a GP may suggest an elimination diet, blood tests or a hydrogen breath test. MedlinePlus describes the hydrogen breath test as the most common test, and says that if breath hydrogen levels rise and symptoms get worse during the test, a doctor may diagnose lactose intolerance.

Because irritable bowel syndrome, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease and small bowel bacterial overgrowth can cause symptoms similar to those of lactose intolerance, a doctor considers these as well, according to MedlinePlus. The NHS advises seeing a GP rather than removing dairy from a child's diet without advice. Anyone with symptoms that keep returning, particularly after eating, can book a routine GP appointment to talk through the options.

sections.heading: How is lactose intolerance managed day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS says most people can manage symptoms by eating less lactose or avoiding it, and that most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet. It says eating smaller portions of foods that contain lactose, or cutting them out, can prevent symptoms. A lactase supplement taken before food or drink that contains lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people.

NIDDK suggests that lactose-free and lactose-reduced milk and milk products may help lower the amount of lactose in the diet. The NHS says that anyone who cannot or chooses not to eat dairy may be at risk of not getting enough calcium, and calcium-fortified plant milks count as a dairy alternative. MedlinePlus lists vitamin D and protein as other nutrients at risk, and suggests asking a health care provider about calcium supplements with vitamin D. The NHS warns against removing foods from anyone's diet without advice from a GP or dietitian.

faqs.q: Is lactose intolerance the same as a milk allergy?
faqs.a: No. The NHS describes milk allergy as a different condition, and lactose intolerance is tied to too little lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose. It causes digestive symptoms such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas. Anyone unsure which applies is advised by the NHS to see a GP if symptoms keep coming back.

faqs.q: Do people with lactose intolerance have to avoid all dairy?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The NHS says most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet, and NIDDK says many people may not need to avoid every food that contains lactose. The NHS warns that cutting out dairy can put calcium intake at risk, so it advises asking a GP or dietitian before removing foods.

faqs.q: Can lactose intolerance go away?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause. When it follows a short diarrhoeal illness, MedlinePlus says lactase levels return to normal within a few weeks. A UK NHS clinical guidance page describes intolerance after gastroenteritis as mainly temporary. MedlinePlus Genetics describes the gradual fall in lactase activity after infancy as occurring in most people.

faqs.q: How do doctors test for lactose intolerance?
faqs.a: The NHS says a GP may suggest an elimination diet, blood tests or a hydrogen breath test. MedlinePlus describes the hydrogen breath test as the most common test. If breath hydrogen levels rise and symptoms get worse during the test, a doctor may diagnose lactose intolerance.

faqs.q: Do lactase supplements work?
faqs.a: The NHS says taking a lactase supplement before having food or drink that contains lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people. NIDDK describes lactase tablets or drops that contain the enzyme that breaks down lactose. The NHS advises asking a GP or dietitian before changing the diet.

vitamin-d-deficiency.name: Vitamin D deficiency
vitamin-d-deficiency.definition: A shortage of vitamin D in the body, which can weaken bones and muscles over time.
vitamin-d-deficiency.overview: Vitamin D deficiency means the body does not get enough vitamin D to stay healthy. The skin makes it from sunlight, and in the UK the sun is too weak between October and early March, while it is difficult to get enough from food alone. Prolonged or severe deficiency can affect the bones and muscles, causing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
causes: Too little vitamin D taken in from food
Reduced sun exposure
Conditions that limit absorption, such as gut or liver disease
Some medicines that affect how vitamin D is handled, such as anticonvulsants
Liver or kidney disease

Gut conditions that limit absorption of vitamin D

vitamin-d-deficiency.diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually by a blood test for 25-hydroxyvitamin D, requested when symptoms or risk factors suggest it. Experts do not fully agree on the level that counts as deficient, and testing everyone is not recommended. If rickets or osteomalacia is suspected, calcium and other bone-related blood tests, and sometimes X-rays, are used.

sections.heading: What is vitamin D deficiency and how does the body get vitamin D?
sections.body:
Vitamin D deficiency means the body does not get enough vitamin D to stay healthy. Low vitamin D can reduce bone density, and severe deficiency can lead to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

The skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to summer sunlight. The NHS says that in the UK, from about late March or early April to the end of September, most people can make enough from sunlight, but from October to early March the sun is too weak. Oily fish, red meat, egg yolks and fortified foods such as some breakfast cereals and fat spreads are the main food sources, and it is difficult to get enough from food alone.

Two common drivers of deficiency are a low intake of foods containing vitamin D and reduced time in the sun. Clinicians do not fully agree on the blood level that should count as deficient. NICE CKS notes there is no clear consensus on the threshold for adults, and different guidelines give different definitions.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of vitamin D deficiency?
sections.body:
In adults, prolonged or severe deficiency can cause bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue and muscle twitching. Osteomalacia, a softening of the bones in adults, causes weak bones, bone pain and muscle weakness, according to MedlinePlus. The NHS lists pain in the back, shoulder, rib, pelvis or leg, trouble climbing stairs or getting up from a chair because of weak muscles, and tingling, cramping or twitching muscles as symptoms of rickets and osteomalacia.

In children, the equivalent bone condition is rickets, and the NHS says bowed legs are the main sign. Children may also have swollen, painful wrists, according to the NHS, and NI Direct adds a waddling walk, thickened ankles, wrists and knees, and poor growth. A StatPearls review adds that children with deficiency may be irritable or lethargic, or have delayed development or fractures.

Low blood calcium can make rickets symptoms worse and can also cause muscle cramps, twitching, tingling in the hands and feet, and fits.

sections.heading: What causes vitamin D deficiency and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
Deficiency tends to arise when too little vitamin D is taken in, too little is made by the skin, or the body cannot absorb or use it well. The NHS says rickets and osteomalacia are usually caused by low levels of vitamin D and calcium in the body.

The NHS says people who rarely go outdoors, live in a care home or usually cover most of their skin outside are less likely to make enough vitamin D from sunlight. People with dark skin, such as those of African, African-Caribbean or South Asian background, may also not make enough from sunlight.

MedlinePlus lists poor absorption of vitamin D in the gut, for example after gastric bypass surgery or because of a gastrointestinal disease, and liver disease, because the liver is needed to turn vitamin D into its active form. The NHS adds that rare forms of kidney, liver and intestinal conditions can affect the absorption of vitamins and minerals in children. MedlinePlus also says that babies who are only breastfed may develop vitamin D deficiency.

sections.heading: How is vitamin D deficiency diagnosed?
sections.body:
Vitamin D status is measured with a blood test for 25-hydroxyvitamin D. The NHS says a GP will typically check vitamin D and calcium levels when rickets or osteomalacia is suspected, and may order X-rays or bone scans.

NICE CKS says universal screening is recommended only when there are musculoskeletal symptoms that could be due to vitamin D deficiency. NICE public health guidance similarly advises testing only people with symptoms of deficiency or at very high risk, so testing everyone is not recommended. The clinician decides whether a test is needed.

MedlinePlus says blood tests for osteomalacia check vitamin D, calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone levels. Because experts do not fully agree on the level that counts as deficient, definitions differ between guidelines. NICE CKS notes there is no clear consensus on the threshold used for adults.

sections.heading: How is vitamin D deficiency treated and prevented?
sections.body:
Treatment of rickets and osteomalacia usually aims to raise vitamin D and calcium, by eating foods rich in them or taking daily supplements, according to the NHS. MedlinePlus says treatment may involve vitamin D, calcium and phosphorus supplements taken by mouth, and that sun exposure helps prevent deficiency. NICE CKS says follow-up is used to assess for toxicity, which usually shows as a high blood calcium.

The NHS advises that everyone should consider a daily vitamin D supplement during the autumn and winter, because it is difficult to get enough from food alone. Some groups are advised to take one all year, including people who are not often outdoors, people in institutions such as care homes, and people who usually cover most of their skin outdoors. The NHS says vitamin D overdose cannot happen through sunlight, but skin still needs protection from sunburn. Too much vitamin D from supplements can raise the calcium level in the blood, which is why doses are monitored.

sections.heading: When should you see a doctor about low vitamin D?
sections.body:
The NHS says an adult with bone pain or muscle weakness should see a GP to get it checked. It says the same for a child with signs of rickets, such as bone pain, delayed growth, muscle weakness or skeletal problems. A routine GP appointment is the usual route. The GP will check vitamin D and calcium levels and may order X-rays and bone scans.

Call NHS 111 or contact the GP the same day for muscle cramps or spasms that are new and unexplained. Call 999 for a seizure.

People who think they are at higher risk can ask the GP or pharmacist whether a supplement is suitable for them. The NHS advises a supplement all year for people who are not often outdoors, people in care homes and people who usually cover most of their skin outdoors. Supplements should not be taken in excess, because too much vitamin D can raise blood calcium.

faqs.q: Can vitamin D deficiency be corrected?
faqs.a: Treatment usually aims to raise vitamin D with supplements, alongside diet and sun exposure. NICE CKS describes follow-up to assess for toxicity, which usually shows as a high blood calcium. Whether symptoms such as bone pain improve depends on the person and the cause, and a GP can advise.

faqs.q: Does low vitamin D make you tired?
faqs.a: Fatigue is listed among the symptoms of prolonged or severe vitamin D deficiency. Tiredness has many possible causes, so it does not on its own show that vitamin D is low. A GP can look for other causes and can arrange a blood test if symptoms or risk factors suggest low vitamin D.

faqs.q: Can you get enough vitamin D from sunlight in the UK?
faqs.a: In the summer months the skin can make vitamin D from sunlight. The NHS says the UK sun is too weak to make enough from October to early March. The NHS advises everyone to consider a daily supplement during autumn and winter, and some people are advised to take one all year. Skin still needs protection from sunburn.

faqs.q: Can you take too much vitamin D?
faqs.a: Yes, too much vitamin D, almost always from supplements, can raise calcium in the blood, which is why doses are monitored. The NHS says sunlight cannot cause a vitamin D overdose. A pharmacist or GP can advise on suitable products and amounts.

faqs.q: Who should have a vitamin D blood test?
faqs.a: NICE CKS says universal screening is recommended only when there are musculoskeletal symptoms that could be due to vitamin D deficiency. NICE public health guidance similarly advises testing only people with symptoms of deficiency or at very high risk. The decision is made by the clinician, and testing everyone is not recommended.

faqs.q: What is the difference between rickets and osteomalacia?
faqs.a: Rickets is the childhood condition, in which bones soften before growth is complete, and osteomalacia is the adult form. The NHS says bowed legs are the main sign of rickets, while osteomalacia brings bone pain and muscle weakness. Both are usually caused by low levels of vitamin D and calcium. A GP can check vitamin D and calcium levels if either is suspected.

vitamin-b12-deficiency.name: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anaemia
vitamin-b12-deficiency.definition: A lack of vitamin B12 or folate that affects the body's ability to make fully working red blood cells.
vitamin-b12-deficiency.overview: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia happens when a lack of either vitamin affects how the body produces healthy red blood cells. The red blood cells are usually larger than normal, a pattern known as megaloblastic anaemia. Symptoms usually develop gradually and can get worse if the condition is not treated. A lack of vitamin B12 can also affect the brain and nervous system, and some of these effects can happen even when there is no anaemia. Treatment usually replaces the missing vitamin, and the cause is looked into as well.
causes: Pernicious anaemia, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks stomach cells and stops vitamin B12 being absorbed, is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK
A diet that rarely includes meat, fish or dairy foods can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency
Bowel conditions such as Crohn's disease can reduce vitamin B12 absorption
Some medicines, including proton pump inhibitors and metformin, can contribute to vitamin B12 deficiency
Folate deficiency can come from pregnancy, heavy regular drinking of alcohol, or some medicines
riskFactors: Rarely eating meat, fish or dairy foods
Pregnancy, which can cause folate deficiency
Regularly drinking a lot of alcohol
Taking some medicines, such as proton pump inhibitors, metformin or certain anticonvulsants
signs: Larger than normal red blood cells on blood testing
Sore or red tongue, sometimes with mouth ulcers
complications: Nervous system problems from vitamin B12 deficiency, including vision problems, memory loss, pins and needles and loss of co-ordination, some of which can sometimes be irreversible
Low folate in pregnancy is linked with a higher risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida, and with premature birth or low birth weight
Temporary infertility
Heart failure in adults with severe anaemia
A higher risk of stomach cancer in people with pernicious anaemia
vitamin-b12-deficiency.diagnosis: A GP can often make the diagnosis from the symptoms and blood test results. A blood test of total or active vitamin B12 is usually the first test, and a single blood test can be enough to support the diagnosis, although some people need further tests. If autoimmune gastritis is suspected, an anti-intrinsic factor antibody test may be considered. Coeliac disease blood tests may be offered if the cause of the deficiency is unclear. The GP checks vitamin B12 before folic acid treatment starts.
vitamin-b12-deficiency.treatment: Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia is usually treated with injections of vitamin B12 called hydroxocobalamin. Later treatment may be tablets or continuing injections, depending on the cause. Folate deficiency is usually treated with folic acid tablets to build up folate levels. If the underlying cause of folate deficiency continues, folic acid may be needed for longer. Improving the diet can help treat the condition and prevent it coming back in some cases.
vitamin-b12-deficiency.prevention: Eating foods that contain vitamin B12, such as meat, fish, eggs, dairy products and fortified foods, and folate, such as green vegetables like broccoli, Brussels sprouts and peas, can help prevent a lack of either vitamin. The NHS notes that when vitamin B12 deficiency is not caused by diet, injections are usually needed long term.
vitamin-b12-deficiency.seekCare: A routine GP appointment is the usual route for symptoms of anaemia, such as tiredness, breathlessness or a sore tongue. Numbness, tingling, balance problems or memory changes should be raised with the GP promptly, and the GP may refer to a haematologist when the nervous system seems affected. Severe breathlessness or chest pain is an emergency, and the route is to call 999.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia?
sections.body:
The NHS says these anaemias usually develop gradually, but they can get worse if they are not treated. General symptoms include tiredness and low energy, shortness of breath or rapid breathing, headaches, palpitations, indigestion, loss of appetite and diarrhoea. Some people notice problems with their vision, or a sore or red tongue that sometimes comes with mouth ulcers.

Vitamin B12 deficiency can also affect the nerves and brain. Possible effects include numbness, pins and needles, muscle weakness, balance and coordination problems, and mood changes ranging from mild depression or anxiety to confusion. The NHS notes that some of these symptoms can occur with a vitamin B12 or folate deficiency even when there is no anaemia.

NHS inform adds that folate deficiency can bring a reduced sense of taste, as well as numbness and tingling in the hands and feet.

sections.heading: What causes vitamin B12 or folate deficiency?
sections.body:
The NHS describes pernicious anaemia as the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK. In pernicious anaemia the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach, so the body cannot absorb vitamin B12 from food. Diet matters too: meat, fish and dairy foods usually provide enough vitamin B12, but people who rarely eat them can become deficient.

Bowel conditions such as Crohn's disease can also reduce the amount of vitamin B12 the body takes in. Folate deficiency can be linked to pregnancy, because the body needs more, and to regularly drinking a lot of alcohol. The NHS names proton pump inhibitors, metformin and nitrous oxide as medicines or substances linked to low vitamin B12.

It names some anticonvulsants, colestyramine, sulfasalazine and methotrexate as medicines linked to low folate.

sections.heading: How is vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP can often diagnose the condition from the symptoms and the results of blood tests. NICE guidance on vitamin B12 deficiency says a total vitamin B12 or an active vitamin B12 blood test is the usual first test, and a single blood test can be enough to support the diagnosis, although some people need further tests. The NHS notes that some symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency can occur even when there is no anaemia.

If autoimmune gastritis is suspected, NICE says an anti-intrinsic factor antibody test should be considered. Where problems absorbing the vitamin are confirmed or suspected, NICE says treatment with injections can start without waiting for that result. If autoimmune gastritis is still suspected after a negative result, NICE recommends further investigations, such as an anti-gastric parietal cell antibody test. NICE also says to offer coeliac disease blood tests where the cause of the deficiency is unclear.

The NHS says symptoms suggesting that the nervous system has been affected can lead to referral to a haematologist, a blood specialist.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.body:
Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia is usually treated with injections of vitamin B12, called hydroxocobalamin. After the first stage, the plan depends on the cause, and treatment may be tablets or continuing injections. NICE says the choice between injections and tablets depends on the cause of the deficiency. The NHS adds that when the deficiency is not caused by diet, injections are usually needed long term.

Folate deficiency is usually treated with folic acid tablets, which build up folate levels, and the NHS says they usually need to be taken for about 4 months. The NHS says the GP will check vitamin B12 levels before folic acid is started, because folic acid can improve symptoms enough to mask an underlying vitamin B12 deficiency. If the cause of folate deficiency continues, folic acid may be needed for longer, possibly for life.

Improving the diet can help treat the condition and prevent it coming back in some cases.

sections.heading: What complications can it cause?
sections.body:
The NHS describes complications as rare, because the condition can usually be treated easily and effectively. Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause vision problems, memory loss, pins and needles and loss of physical co-ordination, and some of this damage can sometimes be irreversible. Low folate in pregnancy is linked with a higher risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida, and may raise the risk of premature birth or low birth weight.

Vitamin B12 deficiency can sometimes cause temporary infertility. Adults with severe anaemia are at risk of developing heart failure, and the NHS notes that anaemia of any cause can lead to heart and lung complications because the heart struggles to pump oxygen to the vital organs. People with vitamin B12 deficiency caused by pernicious anaemia have an increased risk of stomach cancer.

sections.heading: When should you see a doctor?
sections.body:
Symptoms of anaemia, such as tiredness, breathlessness or a sore tongue, are a reason to contact a GP practice, and a routine appointment is the usual route. The NHS says these anaemias usually develop gradually but can get worse if they are not treated, and that some symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency can occur even when there is no anaemia. A GP can often diagnose the condition from the symptoms and the results of blood tests.

Numbness, tingling, balance problems or memory changes are worth raising with the GP promptly, because the nervous system can be affected. The GP may then refer to a haematologist.

Severe breathlessness or chest pain is an emergency, and the route is to call 999.

faqs.q: Is pernicious anaemia the same as vitamin B12 deficiency?
faqs.a: Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune cause of vitamin B12 deficiency, not another name for it. The immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach, so vitamin B12 from food cannot be absorbed. The NHS describes it as the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK, while diet and bowel conditions such as Crohn's disease are other causes.

faqs.q: Can a vitamin B12 deficiency be treated with folic acid alone?
faqs.a: The NHS says the GP checks vitamin B12 levels before folic acid is started. Folic acid can improve symptoms so much that it hides an underlying vitamin B12 deficiency, which is why the vitamin B12 level is checked first. The two vitamins are therefore considered together.

faqs.q: Can vitamin B12 deficiency affect the nerves?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS lists numbness, pins and needles, muscle weakness, balance and coordination problems and mood changes among the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency. Some of the nerve damage can sometimes be irreversible. A GP may refer to a haematologist when symptoms suggest the nervous system has been affected.

faqs.q: Is vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia permanent?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause. The NHS says that in some cases improving the diet can help treat the condition and prevent it coming back. If the cause is not diet, treatment with vitamin B12 injections may need to continue, and folic acid may be needed for longer if the cause of folate deficiency continues.

faqs.q: Why does folate matter in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says folate deficiency can be linked to pregnancy, because the body needs more of the vitamin. Low folate in pregnancy is linked with a higher risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida, and may raise the risk of premature birth or low birth weight. A midwife or GP is the usual route for questions about folate in pregnancy.

hernia.name: Hernia
hernia.definition: A hernia forms when muscle weakness lets tissue push through.
hernia.overview: Hernias are common, and most occur in the tummy or groin. Some cause a visible lump, while others are internal. Common types include inguinal (groin), femoral (top of the thigh), umbilical (belly button) and hiatus hernias, where part of the stomach moves up into the chest. Many cause few or no symptoms, but a trapped hernia can become a medical emergency.

sections.heading: What is a hernia and which types are there?
sections.body:
A hernia forms when muscle weakness lets tissue push through. Hernias are common, and most occur in the tummy or groin. Some cause a visible lump, while others are internal and cannot be seen from the outside.

An inguinal hernia appears in the groin and is diagnosed from the history and an examination of a lump there. A femoral hernia causes a small lump at the top of the thigh and occurs more often in women than in men. An umbilical hernia is a soft swelling at the belly button. A hiatus hernia is different, because part of the stomach moves up into the chest. In many cases hernias cause no symptoms or very few.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a hernia?
sections.body:
The usual sign is a bulge or lump that may get bigger when the person coughs, sneezes or cries and smaller when they lie down. Many hernias cause little or no pain. Some hernias cause a visible lump, while others are internal, and in many cases there are no or very few symptoms. Some people have discomfort or pain that is worse when standing, straining or lifting heavy objects.

Hiatus hernias typically cause heartburn, acid reflux, bad breath, bloating, feeling sick, and difficulty or pain when swallowing. These are also the symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Some people have a hiatus hernia without knowing and without it causing a problem.

sections.heading: What causes a hernia?
sections.body:
A hernia can form when muscle weakness lets tissue push through. Activities or medical problems that raise pressure on the tissue in the belly wall may contribute, such as long-term constipation and heavy straining. Coughing, heavy lifting, pregnancy, being overweight and smoking are also linked with hernias. Factors that weaken the tissues of the abdominal wall include inherited tendencies, increasing age and smoking.

Inguinal hernias are more common in men, while femoral hernias occur more often in women. For hiatus hernias, MedlinePlus says the risk rises with age, obesity and smoking. Most umbilical hernias in babies and young children close on their own. MedlinePlus notes that there is usually no clear cause of a hernia.

sections.heading: How is a hernia diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP can usually identify a hernia by examining the area. The doctor may ask the person to stand, cough or strain while checking for a bulge. NIDDK says an inguinal hernia is diagnosed from the history and an examination of a lump in the groin, and that imaging tests may be ordered if the diagnosis is not clear after a physical examination.

For a hiatus hernia, if stronger medicines do not work, a GP can send the person for tests. The NHS says to see a GP if hiatus hernia symptoms do not go away, are very bad or getting worse, or if medicines from a pharmacy do not help.

sections.heading: How is a hernia treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on the type of hernia and its symptoms. NIDDK says men whose inguinal hernias cause few or no symptoms may be able to delay surgery, although many of those who delay surgery later develop new or worsening symptoms and need an operation. It also says most people with inguinal hernias will need surgery to repair them.

MedlinePlus adds that surgery is the only treatment that can permanently fix a hernia. For adults with an umbilical hernia, the NHS says the hernia is unlikely to get better by itself, and surgery is generally recommended. Children usually do not need treatment for an umbilical hernia because most close by themselves, and surgery is generally considered if the hernia is large or has not gone by the age of 4 or 5.

sections.heading: What helps a hiatus hernia?
sections.body:
A hiatus hernia is when part of the stomach moves up into the chest. Symptoms can include heartburn, acid reflux, bloating and difficulty or pain when swallowing. Many people manage symptoms with lifestyle changes and medicines from a pharmacy. NHS advice includes eating smaller, more frequent meals, raising the head end of the bed, losing weight if overweight, not eating within 3 or 4 hours of going to bed, and avoiding trigger foods.

Pharmacists may recommend medicines called antacids or alginates, which can help ease symptoms in the short term but do not cure the problem. The NHS advises that prescribed medicine is not stopped without speaking to a doctor first. If these steps do not help, a GP can prescribe stronger medicines. Surgery is usually considered only if other treatments have not worked and very bad symptoms continue.

sections.heading: When is a hernia an emergency?
sections.body:
The main danger is strangulation, when the blood supply to trapped tissue is cut off. This is a medical emergency, and a stuck or strangulated hernia needs emergency surgery. Signs include a bulge that cannot be pushed back in, fever, redness, sudden or severe pain, and nausea and vomiting. The NHS femoral hernia page says to call 999 or go to A&E for very bad tummy pain, being sick, or being unable to pass wind or stools.

For hiatus hernia, indigestion or acid reflux with weight loss without trying, difficulty swallowing, frequent vomiting, blood in vomit or upper tummy pain needs an urgent GP appointment or contact with NHS 111. For a non-urgent concern, the NHS says to see a GP if a hernia is suspected.

faqs.q: Can a hernia go away on its own?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Most umbilical hernias in babies and young children close on their own. In adults, the NHS says an umbilical hernia is unlikely to get better by itself, and surgery is generally recommended. Some people have a hiatus hernia without it causing a problem.

faqs.q: Does a hernia always hurt?
faqs.a: No. Many hernias cause little or no pain. However, pain in or around a hernia, redness or fever can be a sign of strangulation, which is a medical emergency. Very bad tummy pain, being sick, or being unable to pass wind or stools needs 999 or A&E, and other worrying pain needs NHS 111 or a GP the same day.

faqs.q: Does every hernia need surgery?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. NIDDK says men whose inguinal hernias cause few or no symptoms may be able to delay surgery, but most people with inguinal hernias will need surgery. MedlinePlus says surgery is the only treatment that permanently fixes a hernia. A GP can advise on the right approach for each type.

faqs.q: What is a strangulated hernia?
faqs.a: It is a hernia where the blood supply to the trapped tissue is cut off. It is a medical emergency. Warning signs include a bulge that cannot be pushed back in, severe pain, sickness and being unable to pass wind or stools. Call 999 or go to A&E.

faqs.q: Is a hiatus hernia the same as acid reflux?
faqs.a: No, but they are linked. A hiatus hernia is when part of the stomach moves up into the chest. Its symptoms, such as heartburn and acid reflux, are those of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. A GP appointment is the route if symptoms do not go away or pharmacy medicines do not help.

sections.heading: What is sciatica and what does it feel like?
sections.body:
Sciatica is the name given to symptoms that arise when the sciatic nerve is irritated or compressed. This nerve runs from the lower back down to the feet. The NHS describes the symptoms as pain, tingling, numbness or weakness in one leg, usually affecting the bottom and the back of the leg and often including the foot and toes.

One NHS musculoskeletal service says irritation of the nerve roots can cause pain in the buttock, thigh, calf and foot. Versus Arthritis describes pain travelling down the leg as sciatica or referred leg pain, and says gentle exercise started early is likely to help. The NHS also says a person probably does not have sciatica if they have only back pain.

sections.heading: What causes sciatica?
sections.body:
The NHS says a slipped disc is the most common cause of sciatica. Versus Arthritis explains that in this case a disc in the back bulges and presses on a nearby nerve. Other causes listed by the NHS are spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis and an injury to the back. Spinal stenosis is a narrowing of the spaces in the spine, and spondylolisthesis is when one bone in the spine slips out of position.

Research on risk factors points to modifiable influences. In cohort studies, current smoking, obesity and frequent lifting or carrying of heavy objects were linked with hospital admission for sciatica, and whole-body vibration raised the risk among people with obesity. Reviews also note that sciatica is related to age and is rarely seen before 20.

sections.heading: How is sciatica diagnosed?
sections.body:
Sciatica is mainly diagnosed from the person's history and a physical examination. One review calls careful history-taking and examination key to the diagnosis. The straight leg raise is described as the most commonly used test, although on its own it does not reliably tell sciatica from other problems. Clinicians look for red flag features, which prompt a wider search for other causes such as infection or cancer. The review says immediate referral is indicated for suspected cauda equina syndrome.

NICE advises against routinely offering imaging in a non-specialist setting. It suggests considering imaging in specialist settings only if the result is likely to change management. Cauda equina syndrome is diagnosed clinically, usually with imaging support from an MRI scan.

sections.heading: How is sciatica treated?
sections.body:
The NHS lists exercises, painkillers and physiotherapy as the main treatments. A medical review describes initial care as focused on pain management and maintaining function, with reassurance that symptoms usually diminish over time. NICE says people should be given advice and information to support self-management at every stage of treatment. Versus Arthritis notes that a physiotherapist can help oversee an exercise programme and recommend specific exercises.

NHS advice says paracetamol is unlikely to help and that it is unclear how much anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen help. NICE does not recommend gabapentinoids for low back pain, and its evidence review found they did not improve sciatica symptoms. NICE advises against opioids for chronic sciatica, and against traction for low back pain with or without sciatica.

sections.heading: How long does sciatica last, and what if it does not settle?
sections.body:
The NHS says sciatica usually gets better in a few weeks to a few months but can last longer. The NHS suggests staying active, starting gentle exercise and using heat packs on the painful area. Versus Arthritis says most people recover fairly quickly, although in some cases it can take a number of months.

In severe cases that treatments have not helped, the NHS says people may be referred to a hospital specialist for options such as epidural injections or decompression surgery. Versus Arthritis says injections are sometimes used for severe sciatica when other treatments have not worked, and that an operation is sometimes needed to free the nerve. A review of management strategies says discectomy is supported for carefully selected patients whose sciatica from a disc prolapse does not resolve with conservative management. A Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials found that the benefits of epidural steroid injections were small, mainly short term, and may not be clinically important to patients.

sections.heading: When is sciatica an emergency?
sections.body:
The NHS says sciatica on both sides, severe or worsening weakness or numbness in both legs, numbness around the genitals or bottom, and bladder or bowel control problems could be symptoms of a serious back problem that needs hospital treatment as soon as possible. The NHS route is a call to 999 or a visit to A&E, and it advises against driving yourself. Hospital patient information describes cauda equina syndrome as a rare but serious condition in which the nerves at the base of the spine are compressed. Warning signs include pain in both legs with weakness or numbness, numbness in the saddle area, and changes in bladder or bowel control. An Oxford University Hospitals leaflet links early surgery with better outcomes.

Leg pain that is not improving is a different situation, and Versus Arthritis advises seeing a GP if pain does not improve after a few weeks or is getting worse.

faqs.q: Is sciatica the same as a slipped disc?
faqs.a: They are linked but not identical. Sciatica describes the symptoms of an irritated or compressed sciatic nerve, and the NHS says a slipped disc is the most common cause. faqs.a: The NHS suggests staying active, starting gentle exercise and using heat packs on the painful area. Versus Arthritis calls staying active the most important way people can help themselves with back pain. A physiotherapist can help oversee an exercise programme and recommend specific exercises.

faqs.q: Do I need an MRI scan for sciatica?
faqs.a: Sciatica is mainly diagnosed from a person's history and a physical examination. NICE advises against routinely offering imaging in a non-specialist setting and suggests imaging in specialist settings only when the result is likely to change management. Suspected cauda equina syndrome is different: it is diagnosed clinically, usually with imaging support from an MRI scan.
